OPERATION KOMOREBI                                                                          PAPER VII



  How to use this volume

   Part I. The finite quantum seed calculus develops the packet language and states the precise scope
   of the archived formal proof.

   Part II. The strengthened development extends this language through seventy-nine theorem,
   proposition, lemma, and corollary proofs.

   Part III. Six supplements give the detailed mathematical constructions behind the formal proofs,
   followed by three alternative derivations.

   Part IV. Forty worked visual pages connect the formulas to finite models and identify the hypothe-
   ses needed at each continuum boundary.



Reading this edition

A seed is useful only together with the operators allowed to act on it. Paper VII follows that principle
through symmetry packets, quantum circuits, moving projectors, channels, effective dynamics, and
refinement. The finite calculus in Part I supplies the common language. The strengthened development
in Part II gives broader bounded constructions and limit criteria. Part III retains the detailed proof
completions rather than reducing them to a status summary.

The original finite item numbers keep the prefix I. The strengthened development has the prefix II, and
the supplementary constructions have the prefix III. All nine mathematical source parts are retained.
This edition revises their explanatory prose while preserving the mathematical expressions, hypothe-
ses, proof steps, and statement inventory. The accompanying report records the changes. Overlapping
statements and proofs are retained because their hypotheses and uses differ. Their total is not a count
of independent discoveries.

The selected archived formal checkpoint covers nineteen scoped manuscript items. It records 323 ex-
plicit theorem declarations across twenty-five active Lean proof modules. These are different units.
The strengthened Part II is outside that nineteen-item contract. The formal evidence comes from the
archived checkpoint of 6 September 2026. The present prose revision does not report a fresh Lean com-
pilation. Exact hypotheses, declarations, inherited compiler records, and reproduction instructions
appear in the Lean companion.

Five explicitly named conjectures remain open in the finite core: anomaly-free refinement, uniform
Feshbach control, Lorentzian reconstruction, the Einstein infrared limit, and massless spin-two packets.
Bounded direct limits and norm limits provide useful criteria. Each physical target still needs the
additional structure stated in its conjecture.


   Four distinctions to keep in view

  A seed’s algebraic orbit is different from a unitary state-preparation orbit. Compression is different
  from an effective resolvent. A normalized channel is different from an unnormalized error family.
  A finite spectrum is different from a continuum particle interpretation. Keeping these distinctions
   visible makes the later results easier to use.

Read Part I first for the packet grammar and the finite statements. Turn to Part II for bounded operator
transport, spectral and channel constructions, and refinement towers. Use Part III when the geometric
bundle construction or a formal specialization needs more detail. The visual atlas follows the same

Part I Corrected finite quantum seed calculus




  A route through this section

  The finite core starts with seed rank, then resolves symmetry and circuit transfer into packets.
   Its geometric statements use the actual range bundle, including the Lie-bracket term. Its channel
  and Feshbach statements keep normalization and invertibility visible. The three examples below
  introduce those distinctions with exact finite data.



Three exact finite models


A seed remembers multiplicity support

For 𝑀2(ℂ) ⊗𝐼3, a coefficient matrix with rank one generates an orbit of dimension two. A matrix of
rank two generates an orbit of dimension four. Neither single seed spans the full space of dimension six,
because a 2 × 3 matrix cannot have rank three. Two seeds can nevertheless cover all three multiplicity
coordinates together. The example illustrates the finite seed rank formula with 𝑑= 2 and 𝑚= 3.

I.15 Conclusion

The quantum realization of the seed calculus begins with a primitive state and a declared operator
grammar. Symmetry projectors resolve the state and every operator into exact packets. In these co-
ordinates, circuit products become sums over packet paths, and Hamiltonian symmetry appears as a
diagonal block structure. When that symmetry is broken, the resulting transfer is measured by the
leakage estimates.

Moving packets carry a canonical connection and curvature. Channels and measurements act on the
corresponding operator packets, while the conditions for error correction become statements about
compression to the code. Exact elimination retains the influence of hidden sectors through self-energy
and memory.

The finite theory therefore provides a coherent language for

                    seed reachability + symmetry resolution + circuit paths
                 +effective dynamics + geometric transport + constraint diagnostics


A physical continuum theorem remains open. The next required results are anomaly-free refinement,
uniform control of effective operators, Lorentzian reconstruction, the Einstein infrared limit, and a
positive massless spin-two sector. Each requires its own hypotheses and proof. Agreement in a finite

II.1 Introduction

Quantum mechanics repeatedly uses the same operation. A Hilbert space is split into sectors, an opera-
tor is resolved between those sectors, and the pieces are propagated or recombined. Symmetry sectors,
eigenspaces, syndrome spaces, adiabatic subspaces, and retained model spaces are familiar examples.
This article treats them as instances of one finite packet calculus.

The elementary coordinate object is a complete family of orthogonal projectors

                        𝑃𝑎𝑃𝑏= 𝛿𝑎𝑏𝑃𝑎,  ∑ 𝑃𝑎= 𝐼.
                                                          𝑎∈𝐼

Every vector has packet coordinates 𝑃𝑎𝜓. Every operator has transfer blocks

                             𝐴𝑏𝑎= 𝑃𝑏𝐴𝑃𝑎.

These identities are simple. Their value appears when the same coordinates are used across represen-
tation theory, circuits, channels, error correction, effective dynamics, and geometric limits.

Quantum information and operator theory in finite dimensions provide the standard background [18,
27, 3].  Finite group projectors come from character theory [23, 9]. Moving spectral subspaces and
geometric phase originate in the work of Kato, Berry, Wilczek, and Zee [12, 13, 2, 28]. Completely
positive maps and quantum dynamical semigroups are treated in [24, 5, 15, 16]. Exact error correction
is governed by the Knill Laflamme condition [14, 22, 1]. Projection methods and hidden state memory
are linked by the Feshbach, Nakajima, and Zwanzig constructions [8, 17, 29, 4].

The first part begins with quantum seeds. A state is cyclic only relative to a declared observable algebra.
For an algebra in multiplicity form, the local orbit dimension is controlled by the rank of a coefficient
matrix. This recovers the relation between Schmidt rank and the dimension reached by local operations.
The finite group section then constructs central isotypic projectors. Cyclic symmetry gives a sharper
charge selection rule. An operator with charge 𝑞can move a state only from packet 𝑗to packet 𝑗+ 𝑞.

A circuit is resolved by inserting the identity between successive gates. This produces a sum over packet
paths. The target probability contains diagonal path terms and interference between distinct paths.
Symmetry can remove entire path families before any matrix multiplication is performed. Unitarity
gives exact row and column relations among the transfer blocks.

The effective dynamics section returns to ordinary Hilbert space packets. Schur complementation gives
the exact retained resolvent and a frequency dependent self energy. The same hidden block gives a
causal memory kernel in time. For a self adjoint hidden Hamiltonian, the self energy has a fixed sign
in the upper half plane, and the time kernel is positive definite. Uniform spectral separation gives
direct bounds that can be carried through a refinement tower.

The geometric part develops two finite constructions. A strictly positive contraction gives a reflection
positive Hankel kernel, and its logarithm reconstructs a nonnegative Hamiltonian. A finite Laplacian
gives a heat trace from which the spectral dimension is defined at each diffusion scale. The article
proves convergence from periodic lattices to the continuum torus at every fixed positive diffusion time.
Poisson summation then determines the continuum dimension as diffusion time tends to zero.

II.14 Continuum milestones and exact boundary

The finite theorems establish exact identities and criteria for bounded limits. Passing from a finite
transfer model to a continuum theory still requires several separate arguments. This section states
those remaining mathematical tasks.


   Definition II.14.1 (Anomaly free continuum constraint system). A continuum constraint system
   consists of a Hilbert space, a common invariant dense domain 𝒟, and operators 𝐶𝑎on 𝒟.  It is
  anomaly free for prescribed structure coefficients when

                                       [𝐶𝑎, 𝐶𝑏]𝜓= i ∑ 𝑓𝑎𝑏𝐶𝑐𝜓𝑐
                                                                 𝑐

   for every 𝜓∈𝒟, and when the associated gauge evolution is defined on the physical quotient or
   physical subspace.

Norm closure of bounded finite constraints, as in theorem II.13.7, is one special case. It does not treat
unbounded constraints, changing domains, structure functions, or renormalized operator products.


   Definition II.14.2 (Reflection positive Euclidean limit). A reflection positive Euclidean limit re-
   quires a limiting algebra of observables, Euclidean time translations, a reflection operation, and
   correlation functions whose reflected quadratic forms are nonnegative. A field theoretic recon-
   struction also requires the regularity and covariance assumptions needed to construct a Hilbert
   space, a vacuum, and a self adjoint time translation generator.

Theorem II.13.6 shows that positivity of each fixed finite Gram matrix survives pointwise convergence.
It does not prove existence, locality, clustering, or the remaining Osterwalder Schrader axioms.


   Definition II.14.3 (Einstein infrared criterion). A quantum geometric tower meets an Einstein
   infrared criterion only if an effective action is controlled at long wavelengths and has an expansion
  whose leading geometric terms take the form

                                    1
                    Γeff[𝑔] = ∫√|𝑔| (Λ + 16𝜋𝐺𝑅+ controlled higher order terms) d𝑑𝑥.

  Here the volume coefficient includes the sign and normalization written explicitly in the cosmo-
   logical term in Part I. The expansion must respect the limiting gauge identities and must include
  an estimate for the omitted terms on the declared infrared regime.

A spectral dimension close to four does not imply this criterion. A heat trace records eigenvalue growth.
It does not determine the tensor structure, gauge identities, sign, or interaction coefficients of an effec-
tive action.

   Definition II.14.4 (Massless spin two criterion). A positive massless spin two sector requires a
   physical two point function or resolvent with a massless pole in the transverse traceless sector,
   positive residue on physical states, absence of negative norm modes, and compatibility with the
   limiting gauge constraints. Interactions must preserve the constraint structure.

A low energy eigenvalue, a spectral dimension plateau, or a finite rank two tensor packet does not
establish a massless spin two particle.

II.15 Conclusion

A complete packet family gives one coordinate language for finite quantum structure. Group characters
produce symmetry packets. Charged operators obey exact selection rules. Circuits become coherent
sums over packet paths. The canonical moving connection separates geometric transport from physical
mixing. Density matrices and channels use two sided packets, while channel covariance becomes block
preservation on operator space and symmetry of the Choi matrix.

Compression to a code gives a natural error correction obstruction. Its vanishing is the Knill Laflamme
condition. Diagonalizing the resulting coefficient matrix produces orthogonal syndrome packets and
an exact recovery on the error span. Schur Feshbach elimination gives an equally exact description of
hidden Hamiltonian packets. Their frequency response is the self energy, and their time response is a
positive definite memory kernel.

Positive Euclidean transfer gives finite reflection positivity. Periodic lattice heat traces converge to the
continuum torus at every fixed positive diffusion time, and the continuum small time spectral dimen-
sion is recovered after the refinement limit. Constraint closure is measured by a quotient of operator
space, not by compression to the physical kernel.

The theorems for bounded towers show how exact compatibility and summable differences in operator
norm produce limiting quantum evolutions. Their hypotheses also mark the scope of the argument.
Unbounded field Hamiltonians, continuum gauge constraints, reflection positive field measures, the
Einstein infrared action, and a massless spin two sector each require additional theorems. The finite
packet calculus gives a common framework in which those questions can be stated and studied, while
leaving their physical resolution open.

III.26.1 Connection axioms and smoothness

The formal proofs establish range preservation, additivity in the section, linearity over functions in the
vector field argument, and the scalar Leibniz identity

Smooth 𝑃, smooth sections and smooth vector fields give smooth covariant derivatives. Equality of
section germs gives equality of covariant derivatives at the point, so the operation is local.


III.26.2 Smoothness of sections in bundle coordinates

Let 𝑥∈𝑈𝑎. If 𝑃(𝑦)𝑠(𝑦) = 𝑠(𝑦) in a neighborhood of 𝑥, then

                     𝑠is smooth at 𝑥 ⟺  (𝑦↦𝐴𝑎(𝑦)𝑠(𝑦)) is smooth at 𝑥.

The range condition is only local. The proof uses the actual inverse local maps and equality of germs.
It follows that smoothness in bundle coordinates does not depend on the chosen chart.


III.26.3 The local connection and its change of coordinates

For a coordinate function 𝑢valued in ℰ𝑎, define

                                   ∇(𝑎)𝑋𝑢= 𝐴𝑎(𝑃𝐷𝑀(𝐵𝑎𝑢)[𝑋]).

For every overlap point, Lean proves the operator identity

This is proved for arbitrary local coordinate functions. It does not assume that 𝑢was obtained from a
globally smooth section or that a smooth extension has been supplied. Together with the local smooth-
ness criterion, this closes the gluing step left open in the fifth block.


III.27 From differentiated projectors to the two-form

The curvature is defined by the covariant commutator, including the actual manifold Lie bracket. It is not
defined to equal the desired projector expression.


III.27.1 The flat ambient identity is proved in charts

For a smooth vector-valued function 𝑠, the proof identifies directional derivatives with the pullback
into each extended chart. It then proves

                   𝐷𝑀𝑠([𝑋, 𝑌]) = 𝐷𝑀(𝐷𝑀𝑠[𝑌])[𝑋] −𝐷𝑀(𝐷𝑀𝑠[𝑋])[𝑌].

This uses the chart pullback of the actual vector fields and the ordinary differential identity, then trans-
fers the result back to the manifold. The auxiliary module works locally at a point, so the argument
applies within arbitrary open chart domains.

valued form is alternating, additive and homogeneous, and lands in the actual fiber. Constant projector
bundles have zero curvature form.


III.27.4 Geometry and scalar conventions

The main global curvature theorem uses a smooth real manifold without boundary, modeled on a com-
plete normed real space, and bounded real-linear endomorphisms of a complete normed real space.
Finite-dimensional parameter and quantum spaces fall within the corresponding real differential cal-
culus. Complex quantum spaces can be viewed through their underlying real normed spaces. This
block does not introduce a separate typeclass wrapper for complex bundles.

The atlas and global connection constructions also support the more general infrastructure for mod-
els with corners wherever their hypotheses apply. The curvature completion claim concerns the stated
theorem for manifolds without boundary. Extending that curvature result to boundaries or corners
requires further work.


III.27.5 An explicit smooth atlas

The implementation exposes the actual total space, local product homeomorphisms, linear transitions,
smoothness proofs and cocycle laws. It does not register these as a ContMDiffVectorBundle instance. This
is an interface choice. The range bundle atlas, local trivializations, overlap identities, and curvature
formula are all constructed or proved from the stated inputs.

The equivalence for smooth sections and the gauge law make the atlas usable intrinsically. The connec-
tion is also defined with values in fiber(Px). Six constructed objects that contain proof fields, including
both local equivalences and the derivative with values in the fiber, have separate axiom audits.
